_README: Classifier table for per-deployment exhaustion state in `ferry dash`.
Copy to ~/.config/ferry/event-rules.json and replace the placeholder
wording with what YOUR providers actually say. This file is deliberately
data rather than code: adding a provider should not mean editing the ferry
repo, and the repo is public, so a vendor's name, its error wording and its
plan terms belong in your own config and not in version control.
Every value here is a synthetic placeholder. Do not read it as a claim
about any real provider.
HOW A RULE MATCHES. First rule that matches wins, so order matters: put the
specific ones above the general ones. A rule may test any combination of
status           - HTTP status codes, as numbers
message_contains - case-insensitive substrings of the provider's message
type_contains    - substrings of the litellm exception class name
and every condition present must hold. A rule with none of the three is
ignored, because a rule that matches everything is a bug rather than a
catch-all.
AN UNMATCHED FAILURE CLASSIFIES AS `unknown`, NEVER `healthy`. That is the
whole point: a failure you have not written a rule for should be visible as
unrecognised, not quietly reported as fine.
STICKY vs DECAYING. `quota_exhausted` and `auth_dead` are sticky - only a
success on that same deployment clears them, because a weekly quota does
not come back on a timer. Everything else decays after its `ttl` seconds
without recurring.
WHY THE MESSAGE MATTERS. The dashboard shows the provider's own words next
to the state it inferred. If a provider names its window ('weekly', 'per
day'), you see that because the provider said it - it is never guessed from
a status code.

rules._why: A quota is not a rate limit. Same 429, very different meaning: one clears in a minute, the other may not clear this week. The wording is the only thing that separates them, so this rule must sit above the plain-429 rule below.
Payment required is unambiguous - no wording test needed.
A dead key looks like a provider outage until you read the status.
A 403 is overloaded: some providers use it for quota, some for a bad key. Wording decides, and the quota rule above gets first refusal.
Anything left on a 429 is an ordinary rate limit.
The endpoint never answered, so nothing can be said about quota or credentials.
A generic upstream 5xx: the provider is failing but not exhausted.
